questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q1, key p.7.
questions.title: Cause of subacute endocarditis after dental extraction in prior rheumatic valve disease
questions.question: A 45-year-old with prior rheumatic mitral disease develops low-grade fever, weight loss and splinter hemorrhages after a dental extraction. The most likely causative organism is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. S. aureus causes acute, rapidly destructive endocarditis, not this indolent low-grade picture following a dental procedure.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Coxsackie B virus causes myocarditis, not valve-based endocarditis.
explanations.C: Correct. Streptococcus viridans, part of the normal oral flora, is the classic cause of subacute infective endocarditis following a dental procedure such as tooth extraction, when transient bacteraemia lets the organism seed a susceptible, already-damaged valve -- here, a valve scarred by prior rheumatic heart disease. The indolent course (low-grade fever, weight loss, splinter haemorrhages developing gradually) matches the lower virulence of Viridans streptococci compared with S. aureus. This is the textbook link between rheumatic valve disease, dental bacteraemia and subacute Viridans endocarditis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mycobacterium tuberculosis is not a typical cause of infective endocarditis following a dental procedure.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q1, key p.7.
questions.title: Organism identified by non-hemolytic, catalase+/coagulase-, novobiocin-sensitive colonies on a prosthetic valve
questions.question: A patient with a prosthetic valve develops subacute bacteremia. The organism grows as non-hemolytic, catalase positive, coagulase negative colonies and is novobiocin-sensitive. What is the organism?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Staphylococcus saprophyticus is distinguished from the other coagulase-negative staphylococci precisely by being novobiocin-RESISTANT, the opposite of this organism's novobiocin-sensitive result.
explanations.B: Correct. Catalase-positive, coagulase-negative cocci that are novobiocin-sensitive identify Staphylococcus epidermidis. The novobiocin test is the specific laboratory step that separates the coagulase-negative staphylococci from one another: S. saprophyticus is novobiocin-resistant, while S. epidermidis (and most other coagulase-negative staphylococci) are novobiocin-sensitive. On a prosthetic valve, S. epidermidis is a leading cause of indolent, subacute infection via glycocalyx (biofilm) formation on the device surface, fitting this patient's picture exactly.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Viridans streptococci are streptococci, not staphylococci, and would not be described as catalase-positive cocci (streptococci are catalase-negative).
explanations.D: Incorrect. Staphylococcus aureus is coagulase-POSITIVE, the opposite of this organism's coagulase-negative result.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q3, key p.7.
questions.title: Organism causing subacute IE after wisdom-tooth extraction in a patient with congenital heart disease
questions.question: After extraction of a wisdom tooth, an 18-year-old male student he start to complain with a fever, cough, shortness of breath, Fatigue, aching joints, muscles and chills. He has a congenital heart disease that has been under control. Blood culture showed Gram positive cocci. On blood agar the organism produces alpha hemolytic colonies that are catalase negative. Which the following is the most likely organism causing the infection?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Staphylococcus aureus is catalase-POSITIVE, the opposite of this catalase-negative culture result, and it is a cluster-forming coccus, not the alpha-haemolytic streptococcal pattern described.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Staphylococcus epidermidis is also catalase-positive, not catalase-negative, so it does not fit this culture result either.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Streptococcus pneumoniae is alpha-haemolytic and catalase-negative like Viridans, but it is not the classic organism linked to dental-procedure endocarditis in congenital heart disease, and it is optochin-sensitive and bile-soluble, distinguishing it from Viridans.
explanations.D: Correct. Streptococcus viridans, part of normal oral flora, is the classic cause of infective endocarditis following a dental procedure such as wisdom-tooth extraction, and it matches this culture picture exactly: catalase-negative (all streptococci are), alpha-haemolytic on blood agar. A pre-existing congenital heart disease, like rheumatic valve disease, provides the abnormal valve surface that a transient dental bacteraemia can seed. The subacute onset (fever, fatigue, joint and muscle aches developing after the procedure) fits the lower-virulence, indolent course typical of Viridans streptococcal endocarditis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Enterococcus faecalis is more typically linked to genitourinary or GI-procedure bacteraemia, not a dental extraction, and it is not the classic organism in this vignette.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q4, key p.7.
questions.title: Long-term prophylaxis to prevent recurrent rheumatic fever attacks
questions.question: A patient with history of rheumatic fever is asking about preventing recurrent attacks. The most appropriate long-term prophylaxis is:

options.C: No prophylaxis necessary after first attack

explanations.A: Correct. Benzathine penicillin, given as a monthly long-acting intramuscular injection, is the standard secondary prophylaxis used to prevent recurrent attacks of rheumatic fever. Because each further streptococcal pharyngitis risks triggering another bout of immune-mediated cardiac damage, sustained antibiotic levels between doses are needed to prevent the organism from re-establishing itself in the throat; the long-acting depot formulation maintains this cover for about a month per injection, which is why it is dosed monthly rather than daily. This regimen is continued for years, often into adulthood, particularly when carditis has occurred.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Daily oral amoxicillin is not the standard secondary-prophylaxis regimen for rheumatic fever; the long-acting monthly injectable penicillin regimen is preferred for reliable adherence and sustained cover.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Prophylaxis is very much necessary after a first attack, since recurrent rheumatic fever carries a high risk of cumulative, worsening cardiac damage.
explanations.D: Incorrect. A single yearly dose of erythromycin would leave long stretches without adequate antimicrobial cover against recurrent streptococcal infection, unlike the sustained monthly penicillin regimen.

questions.source_citation: CVS Final Microbiology Questions (Mucize Doctors), Q6, key p.7.
questions.title: Long-term RF prophylaxis in a penicillin-allergic patient with recurrent pharyngitis
questions.question: A 16-year-old boy with a history of acute rheumatic fever complicated by mild mitral regurgitation presents to the clinic for follow-up. He reports recurrent episodes of sore throat over the past year. His medical history is significant for a documented immediate hypersensitivity reaction to penicillin. Physical examination is unremarkable except for a soft holosystolic murmur at the apex. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term management to prevent recurrent rheumatic fever and progressive cardiac damage?

options.C: Immediate surgical replacement of the mitral valve
options.D: Short courses of antibiotics only during symptomatic pharyngitis

explanations.A: Incorrect. Benzathine penicillin is the standard first-line prophylaxis, but this patient has a documented immediate (type I) hypersensitivity reaction to penicillin, making it contraindicated here.
explanations.B: Correct. Oral erythromycin is the recommended alternative for long-term secondary prophylaxis against recurrent rheumatic fever in a patient with a documented penicillin allergy. Continuous prophylaxis, rather than treatment only during symptomatic episodes, is needed because streptococcal pharyngitis can be subclinical and still trigger a further rheumatic attack, and this patient already has established mild mitral regurgitation that further attacks would worsen. Substituting erythromycin preserves the same principle of sustained antimicrobial cover against group A Streptococcus while avoiding the contraindicated drug.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Mild mitral regurgitation on examination does not itself warrant immediate surgical valve replacement; the priority here is preventing further rheumatic damage with prophylaxis, not surgery.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Treating only symptomatic episodes would miss subclinical streptococcal infections capable of triggering another rheumatic attack, which is why continuous, not intermittent, prophylaxis is required.

questions.title: Organism identified by poor dental hygiene, rheumatic heart disease and alpha-hemolytic, bile-insoluble, optochin-resistant colonies
questions.question: A patient with poor dental hygiene and a history of rheumatic heart disease presents with low-grade fever, night sweats, and splinter hemorrhages. Blood cultures show alpha-hemolytic colonies that are bile-insoluble and optochin-resistant. Which organism is most likely responsible?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Staphylococcus aureus is not alpha-haemolytic in this classic streptococcal pattern, and it produces an acute, not this subacute, indolent picture.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Streptococcus pneumoniae is alpha-haemolytic but is bile-SOLUBLE and optochin-SENSITIVE, the reverse of the culture results given here.
explanations.C: Correct. Streptococcus viridans, part of the normal oral flora, is the classic cause of subacute infective endocarditis in a patient with poor dental hygiene and a pre-existing damaged valve such as rheumatic heart disease. The laboratory clues confirm it: Viridans streptococci are alpha-haemolytic, bile-insoluble and optochin-resistant, the pattern that distinguishes them from Streptococcus pneumoniae (bile-soluble, optochin-sensitive). The indolent course -- low-grade fever, night sweats and splinter haemorrhages -- matches the lower virulence of Viridans streptococci compared with acute pathogens such as S. aureus.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Enterococcus faecalis is more typically linked to genitourinary or GI-procedure bacteraemia and does not match this optochin-resistant, bile-insoluble alpha-haemolytic laboratory pattern as the classic dental-hygiene-associated organism.

questions.source_citation: Microbiology CVS201 Questions (Final), Q8, key p.9.
questions.title: Organism that is normal flora of the human oropharynx
questions.question: Which of the following organisms is a normal flora of human oropharynx?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Candida albicans can be found in the oral cavity opportunistically but is not considered a defining member of normal oropharyngeal bacterial flora in this context.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Streptococcus pyogenes is a pathogen that can transiently colonise or infect the pharynx (causing streptococcal pharyngitis); it is not itself part of normal resident flora.
explanations.C: Correct. Streptococcus viridans, part of the normal oral flora, resides harmlessly in the oropharynx of essentially everyone, contributing to the local microbial balance without causing disease under normal conditions. It becomes clinically significant only when transient bacteraemia -- classically from a dental procedure -- delivers it to an already-damaged or abnormal heart valve, where it can then cause subacute infective endocarditis. This dual identity, harmless commensal in the mouth versus classic cause of subacute endocarditis once in the bloodstream, is the key teaching point linking oral flora to cardiovascular disease.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Mycoplasma pneumoniae is a respiratory pathogen causing atypical pneumonia, not a member of normal oropharyngeal flora.
